reverse_outline.summary: What the reader will get from the page
Common origin of the failures and the four families that locate them / Patterns link into chains, and lasting repair is at the chain's start
Two customer harms that happened although the provider worked: a promise was booked as fact
The failures share a root in day-one shortcuts that only break later, so nobody is to blame
Patterns link up; the visible money error is the end and the fix belongs at the beginning
Layout of the page and of each entry / The fictional company supplying the examples and what its invented material does and does not prove
Definitions of the four families and why money truth leads / Glossary of five payment terms used in the table
A warning sign must be confirmed by a specific number or record
Double Charge: voiced symptom of a resend after timeout
Double Charge: duplicate approved payments clustering on busy days
Double Charge cause: a timeout treated as failure and retried without a stable idempotency key
Double Charge cost: refunds, support effort and disputes
Double Charge example: renewal retry with fresh keys charged 1,840 members twice
Double Charge fix: single writer, event-derived stored key, timeout kept as unknown
Chapters covering the Double Charge
Phantom Payment: voiced symptom of own status disagreeing with the provider
Phantom Payment: local status diverges from the provider's, with wrong access or reminders
Phantom Payment cause: status written from the response, browser return or silence, though some methods answer late
Where the confirmed record can be found differs between the two providers
Phantom Payment cost: unpaid service, refused payers, figures built on guesses
Phantom Payment example: direct debits marked paid on acceptance, days before collection
Phantom Payment fix: paid only on provider confirmation, explicit pending state, sweep job
Chapters covering the Phantom Payment
Orphaned Refund: voiced symptom of an unattributable debit
Orphaned Refund: late backward money stored as a flag cannot be traced to its funder
Orphaned Refund cause: refunds and chargebacks are separate late transactions arriving after the seller was paid
Orphaned Refund cost: unexplainable balances and unrecoverable refunds
Orphaned Refund example: a refund after payout that the ledger could not record, and its year-end total
Orphaned Refund fix: refunds and disputes as linked records with ledger entries and a funding rule
Chapters covering the Orphaned Refund
Black-Box Balance: voiced symptom of books and provider balances disagreeing
Black-Box Balance: single totals and net payouts nobody can decompose
Black-Box Balance cause: non-payment movements change the balance but a sum over payments misses them
Black-Box Balance cost: audit findings, tracing effort, unexplained seller balances
Black-Box Balance example: the year-end gap of 412,000 euros and its three traced causes
Black-Box Balance fix: entry per movement, itemized reconciliation, owned open items
Chapters covering the Black-Box Balance
Stranded Payout: voiced symptom of a paid payout that never arrived
Stranded Payout: marked paid but absent at the bank, later an unattached credit
Stranded Payout cause: paid only means sent, and a closed record cannot take a bank return
Stranded Payout cost: unpaid sellers, ownerless money, churn
Stranded Payout example: unchecked bank-detail changes led to 412 returned payouts
Stranded Payout fix: four payout states, returns as linked entries, account-holder check
Chapters covering the Stranded Payout
Trusted Doorbell: voiced symptom of reading a missing webhook as non-payment
Trusted Doorbell: state driven directly by events, mishandling duplicates, lateness and silence
Trusted Doorbell cause: test-environment delivery is tidier than what providers actually guarantee
Trusted Doorbell cost: payers treated as unpaid, double release, missed deadlines
Trusted Doorbell example: an expired certificate blocked events for nine hours and locked members out
Trusted Doorbell fix: treat the event as a notification and confirm against the provider's record
Chapters covering the Trusted Doorbell
Version Cliff: voiced symptom of an upgrade breaking a report
Version Cliff: unknown API versions and deferred upgrades landing all at once
Version Cliff cause: the version is set in several unowned places, so skipped releases pile up
Version Cliff cost: silently wrong data rather than outages
Version Cliff example: a library upgrade crossed a breaking release and corrupted revenue reports for six days
Version Cliff fix: an owned version register and scheduled, staged, single-step upgrades
Chapters covering the Version Cliff
Card by Any Other Name: voiced assumption that all methods behave alike
Card by Any Other Name: one card-shaped rule applied to every payment method
Card by Any Other Name cause: a unified API hides that status meaning and reversal rights differ by method
Card by Any Other Name cost: premature access, wrong retry timing, incomparable reports
Card by Any Other Name example: returned debits logged as disputes, and one debit's long reversal windows
Card by Any Other Name fix: per-family rules for paid, access and reversal, with own neutral naming
Chapters covering Card by Any Other Name
Vault Hostage: voiced symptom of being unable to leave because of stored cards
Vault Hostage: only one provider's tokens held, so a second provider cannot charge saved cards
Vault Hostage cause: provider-specific tokens make leaving a slow vault-to-vault transfer
Vault Hostage cost: weak bargaining, failover that skips renewals, cards lost in migration
Vault Hostage example: the rehearsed switch cannot carry stored-card renewals, so an exit sheet is kept per provider
Vault Hostage fix: choose the vault holder early, write the exit plan, ask about network tokens
Chapters covering the Vault Hostage
Card in the Log: voiced symptom of card numbers leaking in through support chat
Card in the Log: card numbers in side channels and unowned scripts on the payment page
Card in the Log cause: hosted fields do not remove the merchant's PCI duty for the surrounding page and systems
Card in the Log cost: wider assessments, unverified attestations, possible card theft
Card in the Log example: seventeen third-party scripts on the payment step, cut to three
Card in the Log fix: hosted fields only, owned script inventory, page security policy, rule for stray card numbers
Chapter covering the Card in the Log
Open Till: voiced dismissal of risk on a one-euro payment
Open Till: an unlimited public payment page flooded with small, mostly declined attempts
Open Till cause: frictionless guest checkout enables card testing, which only endpoint limits can stop
Open Till cost: fees, refunds and a seller taken offline
Open Till example: a weekend of 61,000 stolen-card tests through one booking widget
Open Till fix: limits, guest challenge, per-seller cap and decline alert on payment-starting endpoints
Chapter covering the Open Till
Frozen Seller: voiced surprise at payouts stopping long after verification
Frozen Seller: an approved seller restricted later, discovered via support
Frozen Seller cause: verification is ongoing account state with deadlines that toggle capabilities
Frozen Seller cost: sellers without income, tickets, churn
Frozen Seller example: an announced requirement change met with one unread email paused 230 studios' payouts
Frozen Seller fix: mirror requirements and deadlines, assign owners, inform the seller
Chapters covering the Frozen Seller
Single Rail: voiced admission that the second provider was never exercised
Single Rail: total dependence on one route, with a backup that exists only on paper
Single Rail cause: a second provider duplicates almost everything, so switching is never practised
Single Rail cost: full exposure to outages and double charges from an improvised switch
Single Rail example: two providers without a switch, replaced by a quarterly rehearsed one for the largest studios
Single Rail fix: name dependencies, count only exercised routes, never reroute an unknown-outcome payment
Chapters covering the Single Rail
First of the Month: voiced habit of running all renewals at midnight
First of the Month: a predictable peak sent flat out, with throttled requests miscounted as failed payments
First of the Month cause: providers ration capacity per customer, and a throttle response is not a decline
First of the Month cost: delayed revenue and wrongly targeted payment reminders
First of the Month example: the renewal job hit the rate limit and pushed 7,900 renewals to the next day
First of the Month fix: spread the batch, budget requests, prioritise checkout, treat refusals as no-ops
Chapters covering the First of the Month
Borrowed Blueprint: voiced wish to build for a giant provider's peak figure
Borrowed Blueprint: a small team adopting large-provider architecture from a blog post
Borrowed Blueprint cause: published designs answer the provider's own, often dated, aggregate scale
Borrowed Blueprint cost: months on machinery while the real small fault remains
Borrowed Blueprint example: two proposals borrowed from provider scale and declined as unmeasured problems
Borrowed Blueprint fix: take the rules, and question each design's problem, volume, year and local relevance
Chapters covering the Borrowed Blueprint
Accidental Bank: voiced proposal to hold seller money in the platform's own account
Accidental Bank: seller funds passing through the platform, unchosen liability, or drift into financial products
Accidental Bank cause: possession or control of others' funds triggers licensing, and product ideas hide that
Accidental Bank cost: regulatory exposure and unpriced losses
Accidental Bank example: a refund buffer in the platform's account rejected and rebuilt on provider-held balances
Accidental Bank fix: map the funds flow with holder and loss-bearer per step, and choose liability deliberately
Chapters covering the Accidental Bank
Patterns form three directed chains that begin outside money truth and surface inside it
How interface assumptions lead to wrong payment status, untraceable returns and unexplained figures
How unwatched delegated controls lead to money symptoms, with two exceptions
How peaks, single dependencies and borrowed designs lead to double charges and unchosen losses
One incident traced through a whole chain, showing why the repair program acts at the start rather than refunding or switching provider
Combined lesson: failures show up where money is counted but are decided earlier on your own side, so fix there
The two opening cases identified by pattern and upstream cause / The useful question is present ownership of the assumption, to be asked in three settings
Design review use: trace one payment and test each recorded promise
Incident review use: name the symptom pattern and its upstream source, and assign ownership upstream
Provider evaluation use: probe the behaviours behind the patterns and record non-answers
Hand-off to the next page introducing the fictional company as a whole

results.finding: sections, unit counts and unit forms match the spec

All 130 aligned units compared: each outline summary states the controlling idea of the spec paragraph at the same position, in the spec's order (introduction p01, p02, p129, p03; the sixteen entries with their seven units, eight for The Phantom Payment; the five chain paragraphs; the six closing paragraphs). The two callouts match no spec paragraph and belong to the thesis statement and roadmap placements. Small omissions inside a one-phrase summary (e.g. p100's 'timeouts feed the Double Charge', which the draft does contain) are not mismatches.
Introduction callout (KEY POINTS): three bullets by design, the declared placement of the thesis statement; a callout is a list, not a paragraph, and each bullet holds one idea.

Introduction ¶4 (p03): the outliner needed two summaries (layout of the page / the fictional company and what it proves). On reading it is one roadmap: the Larkfield and evidence sentences develop the 'illustration' element of the entry shape just listed, and the paragraph returns to the plan in its last sentence. Accepted as one idea developed, as the spec declares it.

results.quote: The table below uses five payments terms, and each entry explains its own again.
results.finding: The paragraph does two jobs: it defines the four families and says why money truth leads, then at this sentence turns into a glossary of payments terms that does not develop the family idea. The outliner needed two summaries. The draft does exactly what the spec's controlling idea prescribes (its second sentence adds the glosses to this unit), so the unit structure is at fault: the glossary wants a unit of its own.

Using the Patterns ¶2 (p124): the outliner needed two summaries (the two opening cases named / who owns the assumption, in three situations). On reading it is one line of thought: the cases are named, traced upstream, and the upstream look yields the ownership question; the last sentence announces the next three paragraphs. One idea developed.

All 130 units examined. Introduction units state the thesis (S3 in ¶2, S4 in ¶3); ¶1 and ¶2 of the catalog carry S1 and S2; in every entry the description and example units serve S1, the 'Why it happens' unit S3, the cost, remedy and chapter-link units the remedy on the integrator's side that the section's controlling idea names; the chain units carry S4; the closing units synthesize and apply S1 to S4. No unit is untied.

Examined: the opening scenario (read in the same paragraph: 'Both failures have that shape'); the table (introduced by the family definitions, read by the 'warning sign is a prompt to look' paragraph); Figures 1 to 4 (each has a caption stating what it shows, and the text around Figures 3 and 4 says it again); the sixteen opening quotes (each generalized at once by 'What it looks like'); every provider fact and both quotations in the 'Why it happens' units (each followed by a sentence of consequence, e.g. 'A key generated per attempt protects nothing', 'A record closed at “paid” has nowhere to put the return', 'Neither promises once, in order or always'); the worked Black-Box Balance example; and the sixteen Larkfield cases. The case paragraphs mostly state cause and effect inside the narrative and lean on the mechanism given just before them; the thinnest are The Open Till and The Trusted Doorbell cases, which give figures only, but a reader of the entry is not left asking what they show. One unexplained fact inside a case (the Frozen Studios' account type) is recorded under flow_is_followable, where both readers reported it.

Every transition_in read at its boundary. Introduction: ¶2 opens on 'Failures of this kind ... share an origin' (cause), ¶3 on 'The patterns also chain' (additional support), ¶4 on 'This page names sixteen patterns' (sequence). Catalog: opens on 'The four families say where to look' (elaboration of the promise); ¶2 'a prompt to look, not a verdict' (contrast); the fifteen pattern openings are carried by the parallel sub-heading and the quote, and the units inside an entry by the bold labels, as the spec declares; p130 opens 'Where the confirmed record lives also differs by provider', additional to the difference by method just stated. Chains: 'The catalog treats each pattern alone. In practice one sets up the next' (cause and effect); the three chain paragraphs open in parallel form (elaboration, then similarity); 'Larkfield's 1 November 2026 shows one chain end to end' (example). Closing: 'say one thing that neither says alone' (summary); 'now have names' (example); 'in three situations' with 'In a design review' (elaboration, both sides); 'In an incident review', 'In a provider evaluation' (similarity); 'The next page shows the patterns together in one company' (hand-off).

Post level: both flow readers describe the declared order (catalog, then the chains that need its names, then the uses that need the chains; single patterns to chains to use) and call the position of every section clear; neither would move a section. Both note that the relative order of the integration, trust and platform-and-scale groups is not stated on the page, and both say nothing depends on it.

Section sixteen-patterns: both readers recognize the grouping by family in the table's order, the stated reason for money truth first, and the fixed seven-part entry that puts sign, mechanism, cost and case before remedy and chapters. The lost-thread points inside it are recorded as separate results.

Section how-the-patterns-chain: both readers recognize the lead claim, one chain per paragraph in the catalog's family order, and the Larkfield chain last as the worked instance. The two lost-thread points inside it are recorded as separate results.

results.quote: So the provider switch that Keel rehearses (K8, told under The Single Rail below: each quarter, real payments are sent through a studio's second provider) moves only the payments that bring their own card, from a wallet or typed in
results.finding: Hardest sentence on the page for both readers (read two and three times): it depends on K8 and on a studio having a second provider, both told four entries later, and the gloss sits in a parenthesis between subject and verb. Both readers also had to go back in the next sentence of the same paragraph (Femke de Graaf, the exit sheet and K4 in one sentence, so the list after the colon reads as part of K4). The spec asks for K8 here; the prose can state it plainly first and give the exit sheet its own sentence.
results.corroborated_by: reader-flow-a item 1 and reader-flow-b item 1 (next sentence of the same paragraph: reader-flow-a item 2, reader-flow-b item 2)

results.quote: cited the Black Friday figure of this entry's opening quote against a wave of about 1,000 renewals a minute. Her answer was the per-account limit told under The First of the Month.
results.finding: Both readers had to work out the exchange: the argument and the answer are given as two pointers to other places, the quote's figure is used for a different argument than in the quote, and it is not said why the per-account limit answers him (reader A did the arithmetic and found the wave under the limit). The prose should state his argument and why her answer follows.

results.quote: **Platform and scale** is a dependency, a peak or a regulated role that nobody rehearsed or named.
results.finding: Both readers found that The Borrowed Blueprint is none of the three things its family is defined as, wondered why it is in this family and third in it, and got the answer only in the chains section ('lengthens every chain'). The family definition, the membership and the order are the spec's (thesis claim S2 and the table), so the difficulty is not one the prose created.

results.quote: They were on Stripe, where Larkfield's studios are legacy Custom connected accounts (seller accounts the platform creates and manages) and Larkfield had collected verification data through its own forms since 2017.
results.finding: Both readers met this fact after the story had ended and could not tell what it explains; each had to guess (that owning the forms made the deadline Larkfield's to chase). The sentence needs to say what the fact shows, which the spec's evidence entry does ('nobody at Larkfield owned the deadline').

results.quote: A few links end in wrong money that none of the five names covers, and there the text says what is seen in place of a name.
results.finding: Both readers did not understand this reading instruction where it stands and came back to it after the three chain paragraphs. It is not in the spec's controlling idea for the unit; it wants a concrete instance, or a place after the chains.

results.quote: A Frozen Seller's money sits in a balance the platform cannot explain to its owner, which is a Black-Box Balance seen from the seller's side.
results.finding: Both readers stopped here: in the entry the pause had a known cause (a changed requirement with a deadline), so 'cannot explain' did not match, and the equation with a balance nobody can break down felt forced. The spec asks only that the Frozen Seller end in a balance nobody can explain; the prose asserts the identity without the step that makes it true (the platform does not mirror the requirement, so it cannot tell the studio why its money is held).

results.quote: At year-end 2025 such refunds came to **€317,200** and chargeback fees to €73,500: most of the Unexplained €0.4 Million, the difference between Larkfield's books and its providers' balances that is told under the next pattern.
results.finding: Both readers needed a second pass through this paragraph: it starts on 18 March 2027, steps back to 'Until Keel', then to year-end 2025, and ends on a forward reference; the question 'Whose money pays this?' is left open and it is unclear whether it is asked before or after the fix. Time order inside the paragraph would remove the difficulty.

Both readers stumbled on the closing sentence of the paragraph: the forward reference to the Silent Webhook is glossed, but 'was noticed as this pattern' uses the noticed/started distinction before the chains section has explained it (second reading for A; clear to B only after the chains section).

results.quote: a return is a new ledger entry linked to the payout (K3)
results.finding: Reader A could not hold the Keel decisions in mind: they appear out of numerical order (K1, K2, K3, K3, K3, K2, K7, K8, K4, K4, K6, K8, K5), are never listed, and K3 is worded differently here than in The Orphaned Refund ('every movement gets a ledger entry'). No single use blocked the reader. Only one reader reported it.

Reader A found two subjects under one name: the title and quote are about card numbers in chat and logs, the mechanism and the Larkfield case about scripts on the payment page, and the entry does not say they are two faces of one scope problem; nothing at Larkfield is a card in a log. The quote and the case are both prescribed by the spec (p69, p73). Only one reader reported it.

results.quote: The table below uses five payments terms
results.finding: Six terms are then defined (chargeback, dispute, payout, reserve, token, acquirer); reader B counted twice. Small, real and cheap to fix. Only one reader reported it.

Every term on the spec's does_not_know list is glossed at or before first use (chargeback, dispute, payout, reserve, token and acquirer before the table; idempotency key, settlement report, SEPA Direct Debit and mandate, network tokens, PCI DSS and SAQ A, card testing, capabilities and dunning in their entries). Every Larkfield paragraph is labeled fictional; systems and people are named by role with a clause at first use (renewal job, payment record store, ledger, reconciliation job, webhook receiver, billing integration, booking widget, the named staff); Keel decisions are glossed where first used; no undocumented provider behavior is asserted (absences are stated as 'publishes no limit', 'no ... page I read says'). The terms that are not glossed are recorded as separate results.

results.quote: The front-desk terminals, all on Adyen, stay on one rail.
results.finding: 'Rail' is never explained, though a pattern is named after it and it is used three more times ('payout states, rails, returns', 'new rails', the table). It is a payments word a newcomer does not have; both flow readers reported it. One clause in The Single Rail entry would do.

results.quote: Every payment method is assumed to behave like a card: instant, capturable, refundable, disputable the same way.
results.finding: 'Capturable' (and 'reversals' in the Orphaned Refund row) is used in the table and explained nowhere on the page. The table's wording and the list of terms glossed before it are both fixed by the spec, which omits it.

results.quote: One writer for every call that moves money
results.finding: 'One writer' is not explained; both flow readers guessed at it (a single component allowed to send such calls).

results.quote: A method family on every payment (card, bank redirect, direct debit)
results.finding: 'Bank redirect' is new here (iDEAL was introduced as 'the Dutch bank-transfer method'), so both readers could not tell whether it is the same family; in the same paragraph both found 'reversals get neutral names of your own' cryptic until tied back to the returned debit recorded as `disputed`.
A Larkfield term without its clause: 'drop-in' is not explained and the entry's quote calls the same thing a '€1 trial class'; both readers were unsure what it is.

results.quote: Larkfield also moves its Stripe sign-up to Stripe's embedded onboarding component.
results.finding: 'Stripe's embedded onboarding component' is not explained, and the sentence depends on the unexplained account-type fact of the preceding paragraph; both readers reported it.

The opening starts from two concrete failures in which the provider did nothing wrong, bridges to the introduction's claim, states the thesis in two short paragraphs and gives a roadmap. It is not a placeholder, a restated question, a dictionary definition, a 'dawn of man' opening or a book report.

'Using the Patterns' does not open with 'in conclusion', does not end on a rephrased thesis alone, adds no new subtopic and holds no evidence that belongs in the body; the three uses are the declared take-away and were announced in the roadmap. The 'Sources and Evidence' block after it is end matter.

¶1 states what neither the catalog nor the chains says alone ('a payment failure is recorded in one place and decided in another') and why it matters (a correction to the money alone repeats; the repair is rarely a new provider but a key, a state, a ledger entry, a reconciliation and a named owner).

¶2 returns to the two customers of the opening and names them as the spec's callback requires: a Double Charge traced upstream, and a Phantom Payment that began at a Trusted Doorbell, then asks who owns the assumption now.

The intro-only reader predicted sixteen patterns in four families in the named order, the seven-part entry, then the chains, then three uses (design review, incident review, provider evaluation), with evidence from a declared fictional platform and provider behavior repeated from the chapters' dated sources, in a plain, non-blaming tone. This agrees with the roadmap and the criterion's expected answer.

The cold reader named The Phantom Payment, the money truth family, A Card by Any Other Name (integration) as the upstream pattern, and the remedy direction (state from the provider's record, not the browser; a rule per method for when paid is set), as expected.

The cold reader named the four families and gave each definition in the expected terms (unconfirmed record of money; untested assumption about the interface; control handed over and not watched; dependency, peak or regulated role not rehearsed or named).

The cold reader asked for the provider balance on one date broken down into payments, fees, refunds, disputes and reserves, set against the own ledger for the same date, with the size and age of the unexplained difference, as expected.
